nodes.name: Generalized Fermat curve of type (k,n)
nodes.statement: A closed Riemann surface $S$ is a called a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$, where $k,n \geq 2$ are integers, if it admits a group $H \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n}$ of conformal automorphisms so that the quotient orbifold $S/H$ has genus zero and exactly $(n+1)$ conical points, each one necessarily of order $k$.
nodes.definiendum: generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$
differentia: it admits a group $H \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n}$ of conformal automorphisms so that the quotient orbifold $S/H$ has genus zero and exactly $(n+1)$ conical points
nodes.statement_short: A Riemann surface with a $\mathbb{Z}_k^n$ automorphism group whose quotient is a sphere with $n+1$ cone points of order $k$.

nodes.name: Generalized Fermat group and generalized Fermat pair
nodes.statement: In this case, the group $H$ (respectively, the pair $(S,H)$) is called a generalized Fermat group (respectively, a generalized Fermat pair) of type $(k,n)$.

nodes.name: Genus g_{k,n} of a generalized Fermat curve
nodes.statement: As a consequence of the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, it can be seen that $S$ has genus $$g_{k,n}:=\frac{k^{n-1}((n-1)(k-1)-2)+2}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Hurwitz gives the genus $g_{k,n}$ of a generalized Fermat curve of type $(k,n)$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the generalized Fermat group
nodes.statement: In \cite{FGHL13} it was proved that, for $n=3$ and $k \geq 3$, a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$ has a unique generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n)$ and later, in \cite{HKLP16}, as long $(k-1)(n-1)>2$ (equivalently, $g_{k,n}>1$), this uniqueness property was proved to be true in general.
nodes.origin_citation: Fuertes, Gonzalez-Diez, Hidalgo, Leyton-Alvarez 2013; Hidalgo, Kontogeorgis, Leyton-Alvarez, Paramantzoglou 2016
conclusions: a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$ has a unique generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n)$
nodes.statement_short: A generalized Fermat curve of type $(k,n)$ with $g_{k,n}>1$ has a unique generalized Fermat group.

nodes.name: Derived subgroup uniformizes the generalized Fermat curve
nodes.statement: In fact, if the orbifold $S/H$ is uniformized by the Fuchsian group $\Gamma \cong\langle x_1,...,x_{n+1}: x_1^k=\cdots x_{n+1}^k=x_1\cdots x_{n+1}=1\rangle$, then its derived subgroup $\Gamma'$ is torsion free, it uniformizes $S$ and $H$ corresponds to $\Gamma/\Gamma'$.
assumptions: the orbifold $S/H$ is uniformized by the Fuchsian group $\Gamma \cong\langle x_1,...,x_{n+1}: x_1^k=\cdots x_{n+1}^k=x_1\cdots x_{n+1}=1\rangle$
conclusions: its derived subgroup $\Gamma'$ is torsion free, it uniformizes $S$ and $H$ corresponds to $\Gamma/\Gamma'$

nodes.name: Branch values normalized to infinity, 0, 1, lambda_i
nodes.statement: Up to post-composition by a suitable M\"obius transformation, we may assume the branch values of $\rho$ to be given by $\infty$, $0$, $1$, $\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2}$.

nodes.name: Algebraic model C^k(lambda) of a generalized Fermat curve
nodes.statement: Then, $(S,H)$ is isomorphic to the pair $(\C{k}{n}{\lambda},H)$ (by abuse of notation we use $H$ in both contexts), where \begin{equation} \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}:=\left \{ \begin{array}{rcc} x_0^k+x_1^k+x_2^k&=&0\\ \lambda_1x_0^k+x_1^k+x_3^k&=&0\\ \vdots \hspace{1cm}&\vdots &\vdots\\ \lambda_{n-2}x_0^k+x_1^k+x_n^k&=&0\\ \end{array}\right \}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n, \end{equation} and $H$ is generated by the restrictions of the linear transformations \begin{center} $\varphi_j([x_0:\cdots:x_j:\cdots:x_n]):=[x_0:\cdots:w_kx_j:\cdots:x_n]$, where $w_k:={\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The pair $(S,H)$ is the intersection of $n-1$ Fermat hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^n$ with $H$ generated by coordinate multiplications $\varphi_j$ by $k$-th roots of unity.

nodes.name: Fixed points Fix(phi_j)
nodes.statement: The set of fixed points of $\varphi_j$ in $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is ${\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_j):=F_j \cap \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, where $F_j$ is the hyperplane $\{x_j:=0\}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$.

nodes.name: Set F of fixed points of H
nodes.statement: Set $F:=\cup_{j=0}^n{\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_j)={\mathrm{Fix}}\;H$.

nodes.name: Standard embedding of a generalized Fermat curve
nodes.statement: The above produces an analytic embedding $S \hookrightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$, called the standard embedding of the generalized Fermat curve $S$.

nodes.name: Leopoldt's Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve
nodes.statement: Leopoldt observed that for $k\geq 5$ the points $[1:\alpha: \sqrt[k]{2}\beta], [1:\sqrt[k]{2}\beta:\alpha]$ and $ [\sqrt[k]{2}:\beta: \alpha\beta]$, were $\alpha$ (resp. $\beta$) is a $k$-th root of $1$ (resp. $-1$) are $3k^2$ new Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve (for more information see Rohrlich's article \cite{Roh82}).
conclusions: the points $[1:\alpha: \sqrt[k]{2}\beta], [1:\sqrt[k]{2}\beta:\alpha]$ and $ [\sqrt[k]{2}:\beta: \alpha\beta]$
are $3k^2$ new Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve

nodes.name: Watanabe's additional Weierstrass points for k=6
nodes.statement: In 1999 Watanabe \cite{Wat99} showed that in the case $k=6$ additional Weierstrass points exist.
conclusions: additional Weierstrass points exist

nodes.name: Locus F(k,n) of generalized Fermat curves in moduli space
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ be the locus, in the moduli space ${\mathcal M}_{g_{k,n}}$ of curves of genus $g_{k,n}$, formed by all the (classes) of generalized Fermat curves of type $(k,n)$.

nodes.name: F(k,n) is isomorphic to M_{0,n+1}
nodes.statement: The space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ is isomorphic to the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{0,n+1}$ of the unordered $(n+1)$ punctured sphere (see section $4.2$ of \cite{GHL09}).
conclusions: The space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ is isomorphic to the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{0,n+1}$ of the unordered $(n+1)$ punctured sphere

nodes.name: Parameter domain P_n
nodes.statement: Let us consider the affine variety (in fact, a domain in ${\mathbb C}^{n-2}$) $$\mathcal{P}_n:=\{(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})\in \mbox{(${\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1\}$)}^{n-2}\mid \lambda_i\neq \lambda_j\} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}.$$

nodes.name: Associated (n+1)-tuple gamma
nodes.statement: To each $(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})\in \mathcal{P}_n$ we associate the $(n+1)$-tuple $(\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3,\gamma_4,...,\gamma_{n+1})=(\infty, 0,1,\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$.

nodes.name: Action of S_{n+1} on P_n via Moebius normalization
nodes.statement: Let $T_{\sigma}\in {\rm PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ be the unique M\"obius Transformation satisfying $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(1)})=\infty$, $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(2)})=0$, and $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(3)})=1$, and set $$\sigma \cdot (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2})=(T_{\sigma} (\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(4)}),...,T_{\sigma} (\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(n+1)}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}.$$

nodes.name: Faithfulness of the S_{n+1}-action on P_n
nodes.statement: The above provides an action of ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ as a group of holomorphic automorphisms on ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ $$ \mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\times \mathcal{P}_n\rightarrow \mathcal{P}_n; (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2})\mapsto \sigma \cdot (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2}). $$ The above action is faithful for $n \geq 4$. For $n=3$ there is a subgroup isomorphic to ${\mathbb Z}_{2}^{2}$ acting trivially on ${\mathcal P}_{3}$.

conclusions: The above action is faithful

nodes.name: Isomorphism criterion for generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement: In \cite{GHL09} it was observed that two generalized Fermat curves $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and $\C{k}{n-2}{\mu}$ are isomorphic if and only if $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit.
conclusions: two generalized Fermat curves $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and $\C{k}{n-2}{\mu}$ are isomorphic if and only if $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit
equivalent_conditions: two generalized Fermat curves $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and $\C{k}{n-2}{\mu}$ are isomorphic
$(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit

nodes.name: F(k,n) as geometric quotient P_n/S_{n+1}
nodes.statement: This, in particular, permits us to realize the moduli space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ as a geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$, that is, as a complex (affine) variety and that the canonical projection map $\Pi: \mathcal{P}_n\to \mathcal{P}_n /{\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ is an open morphism.
conclusions: realize the moduli space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ as a geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$
the canonical projection map $\Pi: \mathcal{P}_n\to \mathcal{P}_n /{\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ is an open morphism

nodes.name: Projective smooth curve C
nodes.statement: Let $C \subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a projective smooth curve.

nodes.name: Multiplicity (order of contact) of an l-plane at p
nodes.statement: For a $l$-plane $P\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, $1\leq l\leq n-1$, the multiplicity of $P$ in $p$ is \begin{center} $\mult{P}{C}:=\mbox{Order of contact of $P$ and $C$ in $p$}$.

nodes.name: Osculating l-plane
nodes.statement: It is known that, for each $p \in C$, there exists a unique $l$-plane, called the {\it osculating $l$-plane} and denoted by $\osc{l}{p}$, such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}\geq l+1$, and that there exists at most a finite number of points $p\in C$ such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}> l+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Each point has a unique osculating $l$-plane with contact order at least $l+1$; only finitely many points exceed it.

nodes.name: Hyperosculating point
nodes.statement: We say that $p\in C$ is a hyperosculating point if $$\mult{\osc{n-1}{p}}{C}>n.$$

nodes.name: Weierstrass points are hyperosculating points of the canonical embedding
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a non hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$, then the hyperosculating points of the canonical embedding of $C \hookrightarrow {\mathbb P}^{g-1}$ are exactly its Weierstrass points.
assumptions: $C$ is a non hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$
conclusions: the hyperosculating points of the canonical embedding of $C \hookrightarrow {\mathbb P}^{g-1}$ are exactly its Weierstrass points

nodes.name: Associated maps f_l to the Grassmannian
nodes.statement: As the $l$-planes of ${\mathbb{P}}^n$ are in bijective correspondence with the dimension $(l+1)$ vector subspaces of ${\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}$, we can define the functions $$f_l:C\rightarrow \G{l+1}{n+1}; p\mapsto \osc{l}{p},$$ where $\G{l+1}{n+1}$ is the corresponding Grasmannian manifold.

nodes.name: Natural embedding f_0 and local chart z
nodes.statement: Let $f_0:C\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^n$ be the natural embedding defined by the inclusion $C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$, and let us consider a local chart $z:U\subset C \rightarrow W \subset {\mathbb{C}} $, $z(p)=0$, around the point $p\in C$.

nodes.name: Local holomorphic lift v(z) of f_0
nodes.statement: Then there exists a neighborhood $W'\subset W$ of $0$, and a holomorphic vectorial function $$v:W'\rightarrow {\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}\backslash\{0\}:\;z \mapsto v(z):=(v_0(z),v_1(z),...,v_n(z)),$$ such that $$ f_0(z)=[v_0(z):v_1(z):\cdots:v_n(z)], \quad \mbox{for all $z\in W'$.} $$

nodes.name: Wedge function w(z)
nodes.statement: Let us consider the holomorphic vectorial function $$w:W'\rightarrow \wedge^{l+1}{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}:\; z\mapsto w(z):=v(z)\wedge v'(z)\wedge \cdots \wedge v^{(l)}(z).$$

nodes.name: Associated curves C_l
nodes.statement: The curves $C_l:=f_l(C)$, $0\leq l\leq n-1$ are called the associated curves of $C$.

nodes.name: Ramification indices b_l(p), b_l and degrees d_l
nodes.statement: Let us define the following integers: \begin{itemize} \item $b_l(p)$; the ramification index of $f_l:C\rightarrow C_l$ in the point $p\in C$. \item $b_l=\sum_{p\in C}b_l(p)$; the total ramification index of $f_l:C\rightarrow C_l$. \item $d_l$; the number of osculating $l$-planes of $C$ which intersects a generic $(n-l-1)$-plane of ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$. Observe that $d_0$ is simply the degree of the curve.
nodes.statement_short: Local and total ramification indices of $f_l$, and the number $d_l$ of osculating $l$-planes meeting a generic complementary plane.

nodes.name: Hyperosculation criterion via ramification indices
nodes.statement: The point $p\in C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a hyperosculating point if and only if $\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}b_l(p)\geq 1$.
conclusions: is a hyperosculating point if and only if $\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}b_l(p)\geq 1$
equivalent_conditions: The point $p\in C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a hyperosculating point

nodes.name: Plücker Formulas
nodes.statement: If $C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a curve of genus $g$, then \begin{center} $d_{l+1}-2d_l+d_{l-1}=2g-2-b_l$, for all $1\leq l\leq n-1$, \end{center} where $d_{-1}=d_n=0$.
conclusions: $d_{l+1}-2d_l+d_{l-1}=2g-2-b_l$, for all $1\leq l\leq n-1$
nodes.label: th:plucker

nodes.name: Normal form of f_0 at p
nodes.statement: Making linear changes of coordinates, it is possible to prove that there exists $\varphi\in {\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathbb{P}}^n)\cong \PGL{n+1}{{\mathbb{C}}}$ such that $$ \varphi(f_0(z))=[1: z^{1+\alpha_1}+\cdots: z^{2+\alpha_1+\alpha_2}+\cdots:\cdots :z^{n+\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n}+\cdots]. $$ This is called the normal form of $f_0$ in $p$.
nodes.statement_short: After a projective change of coordinates the local parametrization has coordinates $z^{i+\alpha_1+\dots+\alpha_i}+\cdots$.

nodes.name: Invariance of the exponents alpha_j
nodes.statement: It is possible to verify that the integers $\alpha_j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, only depend on $f_0$ and the point $p\in C$, and neither on the chosen local chart $z$, nor the vectorial function $v(z)$, nor the automorphism $\varphi$.
conclusions: only depend on $f_0$ and the point $p\in C$, and neither on the chosen local chart $z$, nor the vectorial function $v(z)$, nor the automorphism $\varphi$

nodes.name: Ramification indices from the normal form
nodes.statement: In the above, $$ b_l(p):=\alpha_{l+1}, \quad 0\leq l\leq n-1. $$
conclusions: $$ b_l(p):=\alpha_{l+1}, \quad 0\leq l\leq n-1. $$
nodes.label: pr:ind-ram

nodes.name: Gap values from the normal form of the canonical embedding
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$ and $C\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$ is a canonical embedding, then $$ a_i=i+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\alpha_j, \quad 1\leq i\leq g, $$ are the gap values of $p$. In other words, $a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}$ are the only $g$ integers where {\bf there does not exist} a meromorphic function of $C$ with a pole of order $a_i$ in the point $p$ and holomorphic on $C-\{p\}$.
assumptions: $C$ is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$
conclusions: $$ a_i=i+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\alpha_j, \quad 1\leq i\leq g, $$ are the gap values of $p$
nodes.statement_short: For the canonical embedding, the Weierstrass gaps at $p$ are $a_i=i+\sum_{j<i}\alpha_j$.
nodes.label: re:gap-W

nodes.name: Rational maps with indeterminacy in L_(i,j) restrict to morphisms
nodes.statement: Let us consider a generalized Fermat curve of type $(k,n)$ with its respective standard embedding $\xymatrix{\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \ar@^{(->}[r] & {\mathbb{P}}^{n} }$, and a rational map (denoted by the dotted line) $\psi: {\mathbb{P}}^{n} \dashrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{m}$. If there exists $0 \leq i<j\leq n$ such that the linear projective space $L_{(i,j)}:=\{[x_0:\cdots:x_n]|x_i=x_j=0\}$ contains the locus of indeterminacy of the rational map, then (as the intersection $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\cap L_{(i,j)}$ is the empty set) the restriction of $\psi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, $$\xymatrix{ \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \ar@^{(->}[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]&{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\ar@{-->}[r]&{\mathbb{P}}^m},$$ is a well defined morphism.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: A rational map whose indeterminacy lies in some $\{x_i=x_j=0\}$ restricts to a morphism on a generalized Fermat curve, which misses that locus.
nodes.label: re:rest

nodes.name: Projection pi forgetting the last coordinate
nodes.statement: Let us consider the rational map $$\pi: {\mathbb{P}}^{n} \dashrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}: [x_0:\cdots:x_n] \mapsto [x_0:\cdots:x_{n-1}].$$
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Restriction of pi is a morphism
nodes.statement: As the locus of indeterminacy of $\pi$ is the point $[0:\cdots:0:1]\in L_{(0,1)} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, then (by Remark \ref{re:rest}) the restriction of $\pi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a well defined morphism.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
assumptions: the locus of indeterminacy of $\pi$ is the point $[0:\cdots:0:1]\in L_{(0,1)} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$
conclusions: the restriction of $\pi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a well defined morphism

nodes.name: Image of pi is the generalized Fermat curve of type (k,n-1)
nodes.statement: Additionally, $\pi(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}))=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ (when $n=3$, this image curve is the classic Fermat curve $C^k$).
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: $\pi(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}))=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$

nodes.name: pi is a regular branched covering with deck group <phi_n>
nodes.statement: Note that the restricted map $\pi$, is a regular branched covering whose deck covering group is the cyclic group generated the automorphism $$\varphi_n([x_0:\cdots:x_n]):=[x_0:\cdots :\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}x_n],$$ so its branch values are the images of the $k^{n-1}$ fixed points of $\varphi_{n}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: the restricted map $\pi$, is a regular branched covering whose deck covering group is the cyclic group generated the automorphism
its branch values are the images of the $k^{n-1}$ fixed points of $\varphi_{n}$
also_stated_at: Observe that $\pi$ is a Galois branched covering of degree $k$ defined by quotienting by the cyclic group of order $k$ generated by the automorphism $$\varphi_n([x_0:\cdots:x_n]):=[x_0:\cdots:x_{n-1}:w_kx_n], \quad w_k:={\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}.$$

nodes.name: Quotient group is the generalized Fermat group of type (k,n-1)
nodes.statement: The quotient group $H/\langle \varphi_{n}\rangle \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n-1}$ is the generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n-1)$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: The quotient group $H/\langle \varphi_{n}\rangle \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n-1}$ is the generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n-1)$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$

nodes.name: Fixed points of phi_j project to fixed points of the quotient
nodes.statement: The $k^{n-1}$ fixed points of each $\varphi_{j}$ ($j=0,\ldots,n$) are permuted under the action of $\varphi_{n}$ (fixing none of them), and this set is projected under $\pi$ to the set of $k^{n-2}$ fixed points of the quotient class of $\varphi_{j}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: are permuted under the action of $\varphi_{n}$ (fixing none of them)
this set is projected under $\pi$ to the set of $k^{n-2}$ fixed points of the quotient class of $\varphi_{j}$

nodes.name: Normalized hyperosculating point p in Fix(phi_1)
nodes.statement: If $p \in F$, then, by using linear substitutions in the system of equations, we may assume that $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_1)$, that is, $$p:=[1:0:\rho_1:\rho_2:\cdots:\rho_{n-1}],$$ where $\rho_i^{k}=-{\lambda}_{i-1}$, $1\leq i\leq n-1$ (with ${\lambda}_{0}=1$).

nodes.name: Standard embedding f_0 of C^k(lambda)
nodes.statement: Let $f_0:\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^n$ be the standard embedding defined by the inclusion $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$.

nodes.name: Hyperosculating points and ramification indices of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement: \mbox{} \begin{enumerate} \item The set of hyperosculating points of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is $F$. \item If $p\in F$, then $b_1(p)=k-2$ and $b_l(p)=k-1$, $l \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$. \end{enumerate}

conclusions: The set of hyperosculating points of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is $F$.
The set of hyperosculating points of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is $F$.

also_stated_at: In \cite{HKLP16} it was observed that the set hyperosculating points of such standard embeddings is $F$; in particular, these are Weierstrass points of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The hyperosculating points of the standard embedding are exactly $F$, with ramification indices $b_1=k-2$ and $b_l=k-1$ for $l\ge 2$.
nodes.label: th:hyperosc

nodes.name: Normal form of the standard embedding at points of F and off F
nodes.statement: Let $z$ be a local chart of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ around the point $p\in \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$. Then the normal form of $f_0$ in $z(p):=0$ is given as follows. \begin{enumerate} \item If $p\in F$, then $$f_0(z)=[1:z: g_0(z^{k}):g_1(z^{k}):\cdots :g_{i}(z^{k}):\cdots : g_{n-1}(z^{k})],$$ where the $g_i$ are holomorphic functions such that $g_i(z)=z^{i+1}+\cdots+\cdots$. \item If $p\not \in F$, then $$f_0(z)=[1:z: z^2+\cdots :\cdots : z^{(n-1)}+\cdots].$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
assumptions: Let $z$ be a local chart of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ around the point $p\in \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$
conclusions: $$f_0(z)=[1:z: z^2+\cdots :\cdots : z^{(n-1)}+\cdots].$$
$$f_0(z)=[1:z: z^2+\cdots :\cdots : z^{(n-1)}+\cdots].$$

nodes.statement_short: At $p\in F$ the normal form of $f_0$ has all coordinates after $z$ functions of $z^k$; off $F$ it is the generic normal form.
nodes.label: co:hyperosc

nodes.name: Weierstrass weight
nodes.statement: Given a curve $C$, the Weierstrass weight of $p\in C$ is $$w(p):=\sum_{i=1}^{g}(a_i-i),$$ where the $a_i$ are the Weierstrass gaps of $p$ (see Remark \ref{re:gap-W}).
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Homogeneous ideal, coordinate ring and twisting sheaf
nodes.statement: Let $I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}):=\langle x_0^k+x_1^k+x_2^k,...,\lambda_{n-2}x_0^k+x_1^k+x_{n}^k\rangle$ be the homogeneous prime ideal of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ in ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,...,x_n]$, let $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}):={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,...,x_n]/I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$ be the homogeneous coordinate ring of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$. and let $\mathcal{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^n}(m)$, $m\in {\mathbb{Z}}$, be the twisting sheaf; for $m\geq 0$ the sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^n}(m)$ is generated by the forms of degree $m$ of ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,...,x_n]$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Sheaf O_C(m)
nodes.statement: Let us consider the sheaf over $\C{k}{n-1}{\lambda}$ given by $$\mathcal{O}_{\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}}(m):=f_0^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^n}(m),$$ where $f_0:\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is the natural embedding of the generalized Fermat curves.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Graded pieces Gamma(C)_m
nodes.statement: Observe that $H^{0}(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda},\mathcal{O}(m))=\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m$, where $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m$ are the forms of degree $m$ of $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Graded pieces I_m of the ideal
nodes.statement: As $I:=I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$ is a homogeneous prime ideal, we have that $I=\bigoplus_{m\geq 0}I_m$ and $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})= \bigoplus_{m\geq 0}\mathbb{C}[x_0,...,x_n]_m/I_m$, where $I_m$ are the forms of degree $m$ of $I$ (observe that $I_0=\cdots =I_{k-1}=0$).
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Dimension d(m)
nodes.statement: If ${\mathbb{P}}(\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m)$ denotes the projective space associated to the vector space $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m$, then the linear transformation $(\star)$ induces an embedding $${\mathbb{P}}(\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m)\subset {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{C}}[x_0,...,x_n]_m)\cong {\mathbb{P}}^{d(m)},$$ where $d(m)=\binom{n+m}{m}-1$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Canonical sheaf omega_C
nodes.statement: If $C$ is an algebraic curve, then we denote by $\omega_C$ its respective canonical sheaf.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Canonical embedding f_c via the Veronese map of degree r
nodes.statement: As $\omega\cong \mathcal{O}_{\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}}(r)$, $r:=(n-1)(k-1)-2$, (\cite[page 188]{Har77}), the Veronesse map of degree $r$, $\nu_r:{\mathbb{P}}^n\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{d(r)}$, permits us to obtain the canonical embedding $f_c$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: Since $\omega\cong\mathcal{O}(r)$ with $r=(n-1)(k-1)-2$, the degree-$r$ Veronese map composed with $f_0$ gives the canonical embedding $f_c$.

nodes.name: Choice of basis containing x_i^r
nodes.statement:
To define the rational maps $\xymatrix{{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\ar@{-->}[r] &{\mathbb{P}}(\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_r)}$ it is necessary to fix a basis $\mathcal{B}$ of the vector space $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_r)$. Observe that for $(k,n)
eq(2,5)$ the rational map is a well defined morphism. As for $(k,n)
eq(2,5)$ we have that $r
eq k$, there exists a basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_r)$ such that $x_0^r,...,x_n^r\in \mathcal{B}$. In the case $(k,n)=(2,5)$ we can suppose that $x_0^2, x_1^2 \in \mathcal{B}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: Fixing a basis of $\Gamma_r$; for $(k,n)\neq(2,5)$ the map is a morphism and the basis can contain all $x_i^r$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of Gamma_m by powers of x_n; spaces Q(m-j)
nodes.statement: More precisely, as all elements of $p(x_0,x_1,...,x_n)\in \Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m$ can be written uniquely in the form $$p(x_0,x_1,...,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}x_n^{j}q_j(x_0,...,x_{n-1}),$$ where $q_j(x_0,...,x_{n-1})\in \Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_{m-j}$, it follows that the vector space $\Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} )_m$ has the following decomposition $$\displaystyle \Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_m:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{k-1} x_n^{j}Q(m-j),$$ where $Q(m-j)\subset \Gamma(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})_{m-j}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: Writing forms by powers of $x_n$ decomposes $\Gamma_m=\bigoplus_j x_n^j Q(m-j)$.

nodes.name: Basis of Q(r-j) and t_j
nodes.statement: Let us choose a basis $v_0(x_0,...,x_{n-1}),\cdots,v_{t_j}(x_0,...,x_{n-1})$ of the vector space $Q(r-j)$, where $t_j:=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}Q(r-j)-1$, and $0\leq j\leq r-1$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Basis of Q(r-j) can contain x_0^{r-j}, x_1^{r-j}
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Proof that x_0^{r-j}, x_1^{r-j} are independent in Q(r-j)
nodes.statement: In fact, if $x_0^{r-j}, x_1^{r-j}$ are linearly dependent in $Q(r-j)$, then there exists $a\in \mathbb{C}$ such that $x_0^{r-j}+ax_1^{r-j}\in I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$. As $I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$ is a prime ideal, there exists $a'\in \mathbb{C}$ such that $x_0-a'x_1\in I(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda})$, a contradiction since $I_1=0$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a linear relation would, by primality of $I$, put a linear form in $I$, but $I_1=0$.

nodes.name: Morphisms k_j to P(Q(r-j))
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{re:rest}, its restriction to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a well defined morphism, which we denote by the symbol $k_j$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Local form of pi: zeta = z^k
nodes.statement: In particular, the morphism $\pi$ defined in the local chart $z$, around the point $p$, is of the form $$\zeta:=\pi(z)=z^{k}.$$
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Morphisms g_j factoring k_j through pi
nodes.statement: By the construction, we may see that $\pi$ factorizes the morphism $k_j$, and we obtain the following diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \ar[d]^{\pi} \ar@{^{(}->}[rr] \ar@/^1pc/[rrrr]^{k_j} & & {\mathbb{P}}^{n}\ar@{-->}[d]^{\pi} \ar@{-->}[rr]&& {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j)) \\ \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda} \ar@{^{(}->}[rr]\ar@/_3pc/[rrrru]_{g_j} & &{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\ar@{-->}[rru]&&} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: g_j is a well defined morphism
nodes.statement: Analogous to what we have previously seen, the locus of indeterminacy (this can be empty set) of the rational map $\xymatrix{{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\ar@{-->}[r] &{\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))}$ is contained in $L_{(0,1)}:=\{[x_0:\cdots:x_{n-1} |x_0=x_1=0\}$, so $g_j$ is a well defined morphism.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
assumptions: the locus of indeterminacy (this can be empty set) of the rational map $\xymatrix{{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\ar@{-->}[r] &{\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))}$ is contained in $L_{(0,1)}:=\{[x_0:\cdots:x_{n-1} |x_0=x_1=0\}$
conclusions: $g_j$ is a well defined morphism

nodes.name: Dimension of Q(r-j)
nodes.statement: If $s(r-j):= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)$, where $r:=(n-1)(k-1)-2$ and $0\leq j\leq k-1$, then $$s(r-j)=\frac{1}{2} k^{n-2} ((n(k-1) -2 - 2 j)+ \delta_{k-1, j},$$ where $\delta_{k-1, j}$ is the Kronecker delta.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: Dimension formula for $Q(r-j)$ in terms of $k$, $n$, $j$.
nodes.label: pr:dim-s

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: Let us fix a generalized Fermat curve $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, and consider the generalized Fermat curve $S'=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ of type $(n-1,k)$. We note that $$H^{0}(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'}(r-j))\cong Q(r-j).$$ For $m\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, let $h'(m)$ denote the dimension of the global section space $H^{0}(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'}(m))$ over ${\mathbb{C}}$. Recall that $\omega_{S'}\cong \mathcal{O}_{S'}((n-2)(k-1)-2)$. By the Riemann-Roch Formula, $$h'(-k+1+j))-h'(r'-(-k+1+j))=(-k+1+j)k^{n-2}-\left(\frac{k^{n-2} r' +2}{2}\right)+1,$$ where $r':=(n-2)(k-1)-2$. Since $s(r-j)= h'(r'-(-k+1+j))$ and $h'(-k+1+j))=\delta_{k-1, j}$, we obtain the desired equality.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: Identify $Q(r-j)$ with sections on the type-$(k,n-1)$ curve and apply Riemann-Roch.

nodes.name: Lower bound for the Weierstrass weight of hyperosculating points
nodes.statement: Let $p \in F$ and let $w(p)$ be its weight. If $n\geq 3$, then $$\widehat{w}(p):=\frac{1}{24}(k-1) (k^{n-1}-2) (k^{n} + k^{n-1}-12)\leq w(p).$$ Moreover, there exists a dense open set of $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ where equality holds.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: there exists a dense open set of $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ where equality holds
also_stated_at: We provide an optimal lower bound (this being sharp in a dense open set of the moduli space of the generalized Fermat curves) for the Weierstrass weight of these points.
nodes.statement_short: Weierstrass weight of each fixed point is at least $\frac{1}{24}(k-1)(k^{n-1}-2)(k^n+k^{n-1}-12)$, with equality on a dense open subset of moduli.
nodes.label: th:w-peso

nodes.name: Weierstrass weight of hyperosculating points of the classic Fermat curve
nodes.statement: In the case of a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,2)$, $k\geq 4$, (a classic Fermat curve), it is known that (see \cite{Has50,Roh82,Wat99}) the weight of a point $p\in F$ is $w(p)=\frac{1}{24}(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)(k+4)$, which shows that equality in Theorem \ref{th:w-peso} holds for the classic case.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
assumptions: a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,2)$, $k\geq 4$, (a classic Fermat curve)
conclusions: the weight of a point $p\in F$ is $w(p)=\frac{1}{24}(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)(k+4)$
nodes.label: ej:cla-fer

nodes.name: Generalized Fermat curve of type (2,4)
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)=(2,4)$, and $p$ be in $F$. As $H^{0}(C,\omega_C)\cong H^{0}(C,\mathcal{O}_C(1))={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]_1$ (forms of degree $1$ of the polynomial ring ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$), It follows that the map $\xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^{f_c}&{\mathbb{P}}^{4}}$ is the canonical embedding. Using the normal form of $f_{c}$ in $p$, we obtain that the gap values of $p$ are $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_3=3$, $a_4=5$, $a_5=7$. In this way, $\hat{w}(p)=w(p)=3$. Observe that, by virtue of Theorem \ref{th:hyperosc}, in this case the Weierstrass points are exactly the points of hyperosculation $F$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement_short: For type $(2,4)$ the gaps at $p\in F$ are 1,2,3,5,7 so the weight equals the bound 3.
nodes.label: ej:(2,4)

nodes.name: Type (5,3) curve where the bound is not sharp
nodes.statement: Consider the following generalized Fermat curve of the type $(5,3)$ \begin{center} $C^5(-1):=\left \{ \begin{array}{rcc} x_0^5+x_1^5+x_2^5&=&0\\ -x_0^5+x_1^5+x_3^5&=&0 \end{array}\right .$ \end{center} and $p=[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}:0]$. In this case, $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$. In Section \ref{Sec:finalejemplo} we provide a proof of this fact.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.label: ej:bound

nodes.name: Bound not sharp for C^5(-1)
nodes.statement: In this case, $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves
conclusions: $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $$\mho'_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{P}_n \mid D(\lambda_1,..., \lambda_{n-2})\cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \}.$$ As $\Pi: \mho'_j\rightarrow \mho_j$ is an open surjective map (see section \ref{sec:pre-mod-esp}), it suffices to prove that $\mho'_j$ is an open set in the domain ${\mathcal P}_{n} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}$. In the following, when we use the notation $\hat{\lambda}_i$ we suppose that the value of $\lambda_i$ is fixed. Let us first verify that $\mho'_j$ is non-empty. Fix a point $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n-1}$ and consider the slice in ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ given by the points of the form $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}, \lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$. We proceed to see that in such a slice only finitely many points cannot belong to $\mho_{j}$. For it, we only need to observe that $$\{q:=\pi(p)\in \C{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}\mid \lambda_{n-2}\in {\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1, \hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3} \},\; p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}\}$$ has infinitely many points and $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ is a finite set. Now, we proceed to check that $\mho'_{j}$ is open. Let us fix $(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2}) \in \mho'_{j}$. Let $q'\in D(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3})$ be such that $q'\not\in \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}$ such that $\pi(p')=q'$. For each $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$, let us consider a point $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_{n})}\subset \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and set $q=\pi(p)$. Observe that there are no technical problems in supposing that $(p,q)=(p',q')$ when $(\lambda_{1},\cdots, \lambda_{n-2})=(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\cdots, \hat{\lambda}_{n-2})$. Recall that we may assume $p=[1:\rho_1:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$ and $\lambda_{0}=1$. If $z$ is a local chart around $p$, $z(p)=0$, then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_p \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ of $0$, such that the map $f_0:\Omega_p \rightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, defined naturally by the embedding $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, has the form $$ \displaystyle f_0(z)=[1:h_1(z^{k}):h_2(z^{k}): \cdots: h_{n-1}(z^{k}):z],$$ where $h_i(0)=\rho_{i}$. By the construction, there exists a local chart $\zeta$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ around the point $q:=\pi(p)$, and a local parametrization $$\tilde{f}_0:\Omega'_q\subset {\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}:\zeta\mapsto \tilde{f}_0(\zeta)=[1:h_1(\zeta):h_2(\zeta): \cdots: h_{n-1}(\zeta)].$$ Recall that the morphism $\pi$ is defined in local charts as $\zeta=\pi(z)=z^k$. Additionally, if we consider a Taylor expansion of the $h_i(\zeta)$ we can observe that the coefficients are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Now let us consider the map $g_{j}:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$. We note that, using the local parametrization of $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ around the point $q$, a local parametrization of $g_{j}$ around the point $q$ can be found. Let $g_{j}(\zeta):=[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$ be this local parametrization of $g_{j}$, where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$. By construction the coefficients of $h'_i(\zeta)$ are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Given a formal series $l(\zeta)$, let $Tl$ be the vector column formed by all the coefficients of the formal series $l(\zeta)$ until the grade $t_j$. We consider the following analytic function defined over $\mathcal{P}_n$ $$r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\det(T1,Th'_1,...,Th'_{t_j}).$$ Fixing the values $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$, the point $q\in \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ if and only if $r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$ is not zero. As $q'$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$, we have that $r(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2})\neq 0$ (in particular, $r$ is not identically zero). The set $\mho'_j\subset \mathcal{P}_n$, where the analytic function $r$ does not vanish, is the sought after open set.
nodes.statement_short: Non-emptiness via a one-parameter slice; openness since the condition is non-vanishing of an analytic Wronskian-type determinant $r(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 15 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} For each $j \in \{0,\ldots,k-1\}$, the set $\mho_j$ is a dense open set of $\mathcal{M}_{0,n}$; in particular, $\mho$ is also a non-empty dense open set. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let us consider the set $$\mho'_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{P}_n \mid D(\lambda_1,..., \lambda_{n-2})\cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \}.$$ As $\Pi: \mho'_j\rightarrow \mho_j$ is an open surjective map (see section \ref{sec:pre-mod-esp}), it suffices to prove that $\mho'_j$ is an open set in the domain ${\mathcal P}_{n} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}$. In the following, when we use the notation $\hat{\lambda}_i$ we suppose that the value of $\lambda_i$ is fixed. Let us first verify that $\mho'_j$ is non-empty. Fix a point $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n-1}$ and consider the slice in ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ given by the points of the form $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}, \lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$. We proceed to see that in such a slice only finitely many points cannot belong to $\mho_{j}$. For it, we only need to observe that $$\{q:=\pi(p)\in \C{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}\mid \lambda_{n-2}\in {\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1, \hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3} \},\; p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}\}$$ has infinitely many points and $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ is a finite set. Now, we proceed to check that $\mho'_{j}$ is open. Let us fix $(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2}) \in \mho'_{j}$. Let $q'\in D(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3})$ be such that $q'\not\in \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}$ such that $\pi(p')=q'$. For each $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$, let us consider a point $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_{n})}\subset \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and set $q=\pi(p)$. Observe that there are no technical problems in supposing that $(p,q)=(p',q')$ when $(\lambda_{1},\cdots, \lambda_{n-2})=(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\cdots, \hat{\lambda}_{n-2})$. Recall that we may assume $p=[1:\rho_1:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$ and $\lambda_{0}=1$. If $z$ is a local chart around $p$, $z(p)=0$, then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_p \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ of $0$, such that the map $f_0:\Omega_p \rightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, defined naturally by the embedding $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, has the form $$ \displaystyle f_0(z)=[1:h_1(z^{k}):h_2(z^{k}): \cdots: h_{n-1}(z^{k}):z],$$ where $h_i(0)=\rho_{i}$. By the construction, there exists a local chart $\zeta$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ around the point $q:=\pi(p)$, and a local parametrization $$\tilde{f}_0:\Omega'_q\subset {\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}:\zeta\mapsto \tilde{f}_0(\zeta)=[1:h_1(\zeta):h_2(\zeta): \cdots: h_{n-1}(\zeta)].$$ Recall that the morphism $\pi$ is defined in local charts as $\zeta=\pi(z)=z^k$. Additionally, if we consider a Taylor expansion of the $h_i(\zeta)$ we can observe that the coefficients are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Now let us consider the map $g_{j}:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$. We note that, using the local parametrization of $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ around the point $q$, a local parametrization of $g_{j}$ around the point $q$ can be found. Let $g_{j}(\zeta):=[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$ be this local parametrization of $g_{j}$, where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$. By construction the coefficients of $h'_i(\zeta)$ are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Given a formal series $l(\zeta)$, let $Tl$ be the vector column formed by all the coefficients of the formal series $l(\zeta)$ until the grade $t_j$. We consider the following analytic function defined over $\mathcal{P}_n$ $$r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\det(T1,Th'_1,...,Th'_{t_j}).$$ Fixing the values $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$, the point $q\in \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ if and only if $r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$ is not zero. As $q'$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$, we have that $r(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2})\neq 0$ (in particular, $r$ is not identically zero). The set $\mho'_j\subset \mathcal{P}_n$, where the analytic function $r$ does not vanish, is the sought after open set. \end{proof}

nodes.statement: Now, let us recall the map: $$\xymatrix{ \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda} \ar[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{g_j}&{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\ar@{-->}[r]&{\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))}, \quad 0\leq j \leq r-1,$$ where $r=(n-1)(k-1)-2$, $Q(r-j)$ is the ${\mathbb{C}}$-vector space of the proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}. Considering an automorphism of $ {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$, we can obtain the normal form of $g_j$ in $\pi(p)$: $$g_{j}(\zeta)=[1:g_{(1\; j)}(\zeta):g_{(2\;j)}(v):\cdots :g_{(t_j\;j)}(\zeta)],$$ where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$, and the following inequalities are satisfied for each $0\leq j\leq r-1$: $$(\star) \left \{\begin{array}{lll} i\leq l_i:= {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all}& 1\leq i\leq t_j,\\ {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v)< {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i+1\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all} & i\geq 1. \end{array} \right.$$

nodes.name: Plan: two cases
nodes.statement: The idea of the rest of the proof is to construct the normal form of the canonical embedding $f_c:\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$ in the point $p$ using the functions $g_{(i\; j)}$. We divide the proof into two cases: \begin{enumerate} \item[] {\bf Case 1:} $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$. \item[] {\bf Case 2:} $(n-1)(k-1)-2\geq k$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Plan: build the normal form of $f_c$ from the $g_{(i\,j)}$, in two cases.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1:} Let us suppose that $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$; that is $(k,n) \in \{(2,4),(3,3)\}$. In example \ref{ej:(2,4)} we have analyzed the case $(k,n)=(2,4)$. Let us consider a generalized Fermat curve $C^3(\lambda)$ of type $(3,3)$ and the morphism $\pi:C^3(\lambda)\rightarrow C^3$ , previously defined. Observe that $H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\omega)\cong H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\mathcal{O}(2))={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]_2$ (forms of degree $2$ of the polynomial ring ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$). Then, the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given by the following composition: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^3(\lambda) \ar[r]_{f}\ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{f_c} &{\mathbb{P}}^{3}\ar[r]_{\nu_{2}}&{\mathbb{P}}^9} $. \end{center} Now let us consider the following morphism: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^{3} \ar[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{g :=\nu_{2}\circ \tilde{f}_0}&{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\ar[r]&{\mathbb{P}}(Q(2))\cong {\mathbb{P}}^5}$, \end{center} where $Q(2)$ is the ${\mathbb{C}}$-vector space of Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, $\tilde{f}_0$ the natural embedding of $C^{3}$. Let us consider the normal form of $\tilde{f}_0$, and of $g$: \begin{center} $\tilde{f}_{0}(\zeta)=[1:\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(\zeta):\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(\zeta)]$, $g(\zeta)=[1:g_{1}(\zeta):g_{2}(\zeta):\cdots :g_{5}(\zeta)]$, \end{center} When $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of $\tilde{f}_0:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^2$, we obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} \tilde{f}_{(0\;i)}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 2$. We also obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{i}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 4$ and ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)\geq 5$. Observe that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)=5$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. As in this case, $\zeta:=\pi(z):=z^3$, if we define the functions \begin{center} $h_{i}(z):=\left \{ \begin{array}{ccc} g_{i}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=1,\\ z\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=2,\\ g_2(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=3,\\ \tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3)\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=4,\\ g_{i-2}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & 5\leq i\leq 7, \end{array} \right.$ \end{center} then the normal form of the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given as $$f_{c}(z)=[1:z:z^2:h_1(z):\cdots :h_{7}(z)].$$ Additionally, we obtain $$a_i=i, \; 1\leq i\leq 5, \; a_6=7,\; a_7=8,\; a_8=10,\; a_9 = 13, \; a_{10} \geq 16,$$ so $\hat{w}(p)=14\leq w(p)$. The equality is fulfilled when $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. The proof, for this situation, now follows from Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski}.
nodes.statement_short: Case $(k,n)\in\{(2,4),(3,3)\}$: direct computation.

nodes.name: Case 1 opener
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1:} Let us suppose that $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$; that is $(k,n) \in \{(2,4),(3,3)\}$. In example \ref{ej:(2,4)} we have analyzed the case $(k,n)=(2,4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Small cases; $(2,4)$ was Example 13.

nodes.name: Canonical embedding of type (3,3)
nodes.statement: Let us consider a generalized Fermat curve $C^3(\lambda)$ of type $(3,3)$ and the morphism $\pi:C^3(\lambda)\rightarrow C^3$ , previously defined. Observe that $H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\omega)\cong H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\mathcal{O}(2))={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]_2$ (forms of degree $2$ of the polynomial ring ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$). Then, the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given by the following composition: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^3(\lambda) \ar[r]_{f}\ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{f_c} &{\mathbb{P}}^{3}\ar[r]_{\nu_{2}}&{\mathbb{P}}^9} $.
nodes.statement_short: For type $(3,3)$, $f_c=\nu_2\circ f$.

nodes.name: Morphism g on C^3
nodes.statement: Now let us consider the following morphism: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^{3} \ar[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{g :=\nu_{2}\circ \tilde{f}_0}&{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\ar[r]&{\mathbb{P}}(Q(2))\cong {\mathbb{P}}^5}$, \end{center} where $Q(2)$ is the ${\mathbb{C}}$-vector space of Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, $\tilde{f}_0$ the natural embedding of $C^{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $g=\nu_2\circ\tilde f_0$ into $\mathbb{P}(Q(2))$.

nodes.name: Orders of normal forms
nodes.statement: Let us consider the normal form of $\tilde{f}_0$, and of $g$: \begin{center} $\tilde{f}_{0}(\zeta)=[1:\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(\zeta):\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(\zeta)]$, $g(\zeta)=[1:g_{1}(\zeta):g_{2}(\zeta):\cdots :g_{5}(\zeta)]$, \end{center} When $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of $\tilde{f}_0:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^2$, we obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} \tilde{f}_{(0\;i)}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 2$. We also obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{i}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 4$ and ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)\geq 5$.
nodes.statement_short: Orders of the normal-form coordinates.

nodes.name: Normal form of f_c
nodes.statement: Observe that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)=5$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. As in this case, $\zeta:=\pi(z):=z^3$, if we define the functions \begin{center} $h_{i}(z):=\left \{ \begin{array}{ccc} g_{i}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=1,\\ z\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=2,\\ g_2(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=3,\\ \tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3)\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=4,\\ g_{i-2}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & 5\leq i\leq 7, \end{array} \right.$ \end{center} then the normal form of the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given as $$f_{c}(z)=[1:z:z^2:h_1(z):\cdots :h_{7}(z)].$$
nodes.statement_short: Assemble the normal form of $f_c$ via $\zeta=z^3$.

nodes.name: Gaps and weight 14
nodes.statement: Additionally, we obtain $$a_i=i, \; 1\leq i\leq 5, \; a_6=7,\; a_7=8,\; a_8=10,\; a_9 = 13, \; a_{10} \geq 16,$$ so $\hat{w}(p)=14\leq w(p)$. The equality is fulfilled when $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. The proof, for this situation, now follows from Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski}.
nodes.statement_short: Gaps give $\hat w=14\le w$, equality generically by Lemma 15.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2:} In the rest of we assume that $(n-1)(k-1)-2\geq k$, and we define the functions $$h_{(i\;j)}(z):=z^jg_{(i\;j)}(z^k),\; 0\leq j\leq k-1,\; 1\leq i \leq t_{j}.$$ Considering an automorphism of ${\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$, where $g$ is the genus of $S$, we can suppose that the canonical embedding $f$ around the point $p$ is $$\tiny f(z):= [1:\cdots:z^{k-1}: h_{(1\;0)}(z):\cdots:h_{(1\;k-1)}(z):h_{(2\;0)}(z):\cdots: h_{(r\;k-2)}(z):$$$$:h_{(r+1\;0)}(z): \cdots:h_{(t_0\;0)}(z)],$$ where $r=t_{k-1}+1$. Let $a_i$, $1\leq i\leq$ be the gap values of $p$. Since $ki+j\leq kl_i+j={\mathrm{Ord}} h_{(i\;j)}(z)$, $1\leq j \leq k-1$ and $1\leq i\leq t_j$, the following inequality is obtained $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)\leq \sum_{i=1}^{g}a_{i}.$$ By Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, we have $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}=\frac{1}{24} (k-1) (k^{n-1}-2) (k^{n} + k^{n-1}-12),$$ from which we obtain the inequality part of the theorem, as the weight of the point $p$ is $$w(p):=\sum_{i=1}^{g}a_i-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}.$$ \begin{remark} Observe that, for each $0\leq j\leq k-1$, $l_i=i$, for each $1\leq i\leq t_j$, if and only if $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$. Combining this with Remark \ref{re:li=i} we obtain that $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the morphism $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$ for all $0\leq j\leq k-1$. \end{remark} As the set $\mho$ of the Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski} satisfies the condition of the previous remark, this finishes the proof of the last part of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Case $r\ge k$: general construction.

nodes.name: Define h_(i j)
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2:} In the rest of we assume that $(n-1)(k-1)-2\geq k$, and we define the functions $$h_{(i\;j)}(z):=z^jg_{(i\;j)}(z^k),\; 0\leq j\leq k-1,\; 1\leq i \leq t_{j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define $h_{(i\,j)}(z)=z^j g_{(i\,j)}(z^k)$.

nodes.name: Normal form of canonical embedding
nodes.statement: Considering an automorphism of ${\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$, where $g$ is the genus of $S$, we can suppose that the canonical embedding $f$ around the point $p$ is $$\tiny f(z):= [1:\cdots:z^{k-1}: h_{(1\;0)}(z):\cdots:h_{(1\;k-1)}(z):h_{(2\;0)}(z):\cdots: h_{(r\;k-2)}(z):$$$$:h_{(r+1\;0)}(z): \cdots:h_{(t_0\;0)}(z)],$$ where $r=t_{k-1}+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Canonical embedding at $p$ in coordinates $h_{(i\,j)}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for gap sum
nodes.statement: Let $a_i$, $1\leq i\leq$ be the gap values of $p$. Since $ki+j\leq kl_i+j={\mathrm{Ord}} h_{(i\;j)}(z)$, $1\leq j \leq k-1$ and $1\leq i\leq t_j$, the following inequality is obtained $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)\leq \sum_{i=1}^{g}a_{i}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Orders give a lower bound on the sum of gaps.

nodes.name: Evaluate via Proposition 10
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, we have $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}=\frac{1}{24} (k-1) (k^{n-1}-2) (k^{n} + k^{n-1}-12),$$ from which we obtain the inequality part of the theorem, as the weight of the point $p$ is $$w(p):=\sum_{i=1}^{g}a_i-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 10 evaluates the sum, giving the inequality.

nodes.name: Remark 17
nodes.statement: \begin{remark} Observe that, for each $0\leq j\leq k-1$, $l_i=i$, for each $1\leq i\leq t_j$, if and only if $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$. Combining this with Remark \ref{re:li=i} we obtain that $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the morphism $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$ for all $0\leq j\leq k-1$. \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Inner Remark 17: equality criterion.

nodes.name: Equality on mho
nodes.statement: As the set $\mho$ of the Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski} satisfies the condition of the previous remark, this finishes the proof of the last part of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15's set $\mho$ satisfies the criterion, giving generic equality.

nodes.name: Reduce to P_n
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $$\mho'_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{P}_n \mid D(\lambda_1,..., \lambda_{n-2})\cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \}.$$ As $\Pi: \mho'_j\rightarrow \mho_j$ is an open surjective map (see section \ref{sec:pre-mod-esp}), it suffices to prove that $\mho'_j$ is an open set in the domain ${\mathcal P}_{n} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to prove openness of $\mho'_j$ in $\mathcal{P}_n$.

nodes.name: Non-emptiness
nodes.statement: In the following, when we use the notation $\hat{\lambda}_i$ we suppose that the value of $\lambda_i$ is fixed. Let us first verify that $\mho'_j$ is non-empty. Fix a point $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n-1}$ and consider the slice in ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ given by the points of the form $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}, \lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$. We proceed to see that in such a slice only finitely many points cannot belong to $\mho_{j}$. For it, we only need to observe that $$\{q:=\pi(p)\in \C{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}\mid \lambda_{n-2}\in {\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1, \hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3} \},\; p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}\}$$ has infinitely many points and $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ is a finite set.
nodes.statement_short: On a one-parameter slice only finitely many parameters fail.

nodes.name: Fix base point
nodes.statement: Now, we proceed to check that $\mho'_{j}$ is open. Let us fix $(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2}) \in \mho'_{j}$. Let $q'\in D(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3})$ be such that $q'\not\in \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}$ such that $\pi(p')=q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a parameter in $\mho'_j$ and points $p',q'$.

nodes.name: Family of points p,q
nodes.statement: For each $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$, let us consider a point $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_{n})}\subset \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and set $q=\pi(p)$. Observe that there are no technical problems in supposing that $(p,q)=(p',q')$ when $(\lambda_{1},\cdots, \lambda_{n-2})=(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\cdots, \hat{\lambda}_{n-2})$. Recall that we may assume $p=[1:\rho_1:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$ and $\lambda_{0}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $p,q$ varying with $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Local parametrization of f_0
nodes.statement: If $z$ is a local chart around $p$, $z(p)=0$, then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_p \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ of $0$, such that the map $f_0:\Omega_p \rightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, defined naturally by the embedding $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, has the form $$ \displaystyle f_0(z)=[1:h_1(z^{k}):h_2(z^{k}): \cdots: h_{n-1}(z^{k}):z],$$ where $h_i(0)=\rho_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Local form of $f_0$ in powers of $z^k$.

nodes.name: Local parametrization downstairs
nodes.statement: By the construction, there exists a local chart $\zeta$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ around the point $q:=\pi(p)$, and a local parametrization $$\tilde{f}_0:\Omega'_q\subset {\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}:\zeta\mapsto \tilde{f}_0(\zeta)=[1:h_1(\zeta):h_2(\zeta): \cdots: h_{n-1}(\zeta)].$$
nodes.statement_short: Induced parametrization of the quotient curve.

nodes.name: Analytic dependence of coefficients
nodes.statement: Recall that the morphism $\pi$ is defined in local charts as $\zeta=\pi(z)=z^k$. Additionally, if we consider a Taylor expansion of the $h_i(\zeta)$ we can observe that the coefficients are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor coefficients depend analytically on $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Local parametrization of g_j
nodes.statement: Now let us consider the map $g_{j}:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$. We note that, using the local parametrization of $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ around the point $q$, a local parametrization of $g_{j}$ around the point $q$ can be found. Let $g_{j}(\zeta):=[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$ be this local parametrization of $g_{j}$, where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$. By construction the coefficients of $h'_i(\zeta)$ are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients of $g_j$'s parametrization are analytic in $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Determinant function r
nodes.statement: Given a formal series $l(\zeta)$, let $Tl$ be the vector column formed by all the coefficients of the formal series $l(\zeta)$ until the grade $t_j$. We consider the following analytic function defined over $\mathcal{P}_n$ $$r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\det(T1,Th'_1,...,Th'_{t_j}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Define the analytic determinant $r(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Open set where r does not vanish
nodes.statement: Fixing the values $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$, the point $q\in \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ if and only if $r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$ is not zero. As $q'$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$, we have that $r(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2})\neq 0$ (in particular, $r$ is not identically zero). The set $\mho'_j\subset \mathcal{P}_n$, where the analytic function $r$ does not vanish, is the sought after open set.
nodes.statement_short: $\mho'_j$ is the non-vanishing locus of $r$, hence open.

nodes.name: Set up projection
nodes.statement: Now we will verify that the bound of Theorem \ref{th:w-peso} is not achieved in Example \ref{ej:bound}. Consider the morphism $\pi: C^5(-1)\rightarrow C^5\; :[x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3]\rightarrow [x_0:x_1:x_2].$
nodes.statement_short: Consider the projection $\pi:C^5(-1)\to C^5$.

nodes.name: pi(p) is a Weierstrass point
nodes.statement: As seen in the introduction $[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}]$ is a Weierstrass point of $C^5$, and in particular is a hyperosculating point of $C^5\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(6))$, (this morphism is the canonical embedding).
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(p)$ is a Leopoldt Weierstrass point, hence hyperosculating.

nodes.name: Apply Remark 17
nodes.statement: By virtue of Remark \ref{re:weie-weight} we obtain that $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remark 17 yields strict inequality.
